Dental Implant Infection: Causes, Symptoms and Treatment Options

Understanding why infections may develop around dental implants, the signs to be aware of, and how professional assessment can help protect implant health.

Book Assessment1-Hour Consultation — £80Call 020 71833573

✓ Clinical Implant Assessment · ✓ Tailored Treatment Plans · ✓ Experienced Implant Team

Dental implants are designed to integrate with the jawbone and function like natural tooth roots, providing stable support for replacement teeth. With appropriate care, implants can serve patients well for many years.

However, in some cases, infection may develop in the tissues surrounding an implant. Patients may notice swelling, discomfort, or bleeding around the implant area — symptoms that should not be ignored, but equally should not cause undue alarm.

Early assessment is important to determine the cause of any symptoms and to identify appropriate management options. Professional evaluation can help protect both implant stability and the health of surrounding oral tissues, giving patients the best opportunity to maintain their implant long term.

What Is a Dental Implant Infection?

A dental implant infection refers to an infection that affects the gum tissue or bone surrounding a dental implant. It is most commonly associated with bacterial build-up around the implant site, which can trigger an inflammatory response in the surrounding tissues.

In its early stages, implant infection typically involves inflammation of the gum tissue immediately around the implant — a condition known as peri-implant mucositis. At this stage, the supporting bone is usually unaffected, and the condition may be reversible with appropriate professional care.

If the infection progresses, it may begin to affect the bone that supports the implant — a more advanced condition known as peri-implantitis. This can compromise the foundation of the implant and, without treatment, may affect long-term implant stability.

It is important to note that not all symptoms around an implant indicate infection or implant failure. Discomfort or minor gum changes can have a range of causes, which is why clinical assessment is important for an accurate diagnosis.

Common Causes of Implant Infection

Implant infections can arise from a combination of factors. Understanding the potential causes can help patients take proactive steps to protect their implant health.

Bacterial Plaque Accumulation

Just as natural teeth are susceptible to plaque build-up, so too are dental implants. Bacteria that accumulate around the implant margin can cause inflammation of the surrounding gum tissue. Without regular professional cleaning and diligent home care, this bacterial presence may progress to infection.

Inadequate Oral Hygiene

Implants require consistent and thorough oral hygiene, including brushing, interdental cleaning, and the use of appropriate cleaning aids. Insufficient cleaning around implant sites can allow bacteria to flourish and increase the risk of peri-implant infection.

Gum Disease & Systemic Factors

Patients with a history of gum disease may be at higher risk of developing peri-implant infections. Additionally, systemic health factors such as diabetes, smoking, or conditions that affect the immune system may influence the body's ability to manage bacteria around implant sites.

Restoration Issues & Bite Forces

Poorly fitting restorations, excess cement left beneath the gum line, or excessive bite forces on the implant may contribute to tissue irritation and create conditions that favour bacterial growth. Trauma to the implant area can also be a contributing factor.

Signs and Symptoms of Implant Infection

The signs of a dental implant infection can vary depending on the severity of the condition. Some patients may experience only mild symptoms, while others may notice more pronounced changes. Being aware of possible indicators can help patients seek timely professional advice.

Redness or Swelling

Inflammation of the gum tissue around the implant, presenting as redness, puffiness, or localised swelling, may indicate the early stages of peri-implant infection.

Bleeding on Brushing

Bleeding when brushing or gently touching the gums around an implant is not normal and may suggest underlying inflammation that warrants professional evaluation.

Bad Taste or Discharge

A persistent unpleasant taste in the mouth or discharge (including pus) around the implant site may indicate active infection and should be assessed promptly.

Tenderness or Mobility

Gum tenderness or discomfort around the implant, or any noticeable movement of the implant itself, may indicate advanced infection affecting the supporting structures.

Potential Risks of Untreated Implant Infection

When a peri-implant infection is identified early, it can often be managed effectively through professional intervention. However, if infection is left unaddressed, there are potential consequences that patients should be aware of.

Continued inflammation of the surrounding tissues can cause progressive damage to the gum and the bone that supports the implant. Over time, this may lead to a loss of supporting bone around the implant, weakening the foundation upon which the implant relies for stability.

As bone loss progresses, implant stability may be reduced, and in more advanced cases, there is an increased likelihood of implant failure. At this stage, the implant may need to be removed, and further treatment — potentially including bone grafting — may be required before a replacement implant can be considered.

It is worth noting that the progression from early gum inflammation to advanced bone loss is not inevitable. With appropriate professional care and monitoring, many peri-implant infections can be managed before they reach an advanced stage.

Treatment Approaches for Implant Infection

Treatment for a dental implant infection depends on clinical findings, including the severity of the infection and the extent of any bone involvement. A range of approaches may be considered.

Professional Cleaning Around the Implant

Thorough debridement of the implant surface and surrounding tissues may help manage infection by removing bacterial deposits. Specialised instruments are used to clean without damaging the implant surface. Regular implant maintenance appointments are an important part of ongoing care.

Management of Gum Inflammation

Where infection is limited to the soft tissues, targeted anti-inflammatory or antimicrobial therapies may be used alongside professional cleaning to help manage the condition. Improved oral hygiene techniques may also be recommended to reduce the risk of recurrence.

Restoration Adjustment

If a poorly fitting restoration or excess cement is contributing to the infection, adjusting or replacing the implant crown or bridge may form part of the treatment plan. Ensuring the restoration fits precisely can help reduce bacterial trapping and tissue irritation.

Monitoring & Ongoing Assessment

In some cases, particularly where infection is at an early stage, careful monitoring alongside improved hygiene may be appropriate. Regular review appointments allow clinicians to track the health of the implant and surrounding tissues over time.

Implant Removal & Replacement

In severe cases where infection has caused significant bone loss and the implant can no longer be maintained, implant removal may be necessary. Following healing and, where required, bone grafting, a replacement implant may be considered.

Treatment options vary depending on the extent of infection. A thorough clinical assessment is required before any treatment plan can be recommended.

Importance of Early Professional Assessment

Early diagnosis of a peri-implant infection may help protect implant stability and reduce the need for more extensive treatment. When infection is identified at the mucositis stage — before the supporting bone is affected — it is generally more straightforward to manage.

Assessment typically involves a clinical examination of the gum tissues around the implant, probing to check for deepened pockets, and dental imaging such as digital X-rays to evaluate the condition of the surrounding bone. These findings help the clinician determine the most appropriate course of care.

Treatment planning varies depending on bone health, gum condition, and the patient's overall medical history. What may be appropriate for one patient may not be suitable for another, which is why individualised assessment is essential.

Professional monitoring through regular maintenance appointments helps maintain long-term implant health and allows any changes to be identified early.
